cells.tense: You're standing in the clearing right now, with your hands already working.
cells.verb: keeping what's worth keeping alive, two things at once, without squeezing either
cells.place: in the open ground where something built on a wrong idea just came down
cells.ask: Tell one person what it cost you to let that thing fall, plainly, and let their hearing it be the end of it — so the letting go finishes as a completion, not a loss, and the care you give what's left stays light.
cells.core:
Something that couldn't hold has come down, and you're not mourning it or rebuilding it — you're tending what's still standing. You can see which parts were real and which were propping, and you're giving water to the real parts without gripping them. That's a steady hand in a place most people either panic or go numb.

What this is free to feed next is being seen doing it. Letting go of the false thing took something from you, and nobody has to witness that for it to be true — but if one person does, the release stops being private and gets to be done. Tell someone what it cost. Not for sympathy; for completion. Then the tending goes on, and it doesn't wear you out.
cells.sheetLine: The false thing fell and you're tending what's real. Let someone see what that cost.

cells.tense: You're bracing for the next collapse before the dust from this one has settled.
cells.verb: tending so hard you're trying to keep even the falling parts alive
cells.place: in the clearing where something built on a wrong idea just came down
cells.ask: Before you decide what to save, sit with what actually happened until it's finished landing — then let yourself picture what the open ground could hold. The care comes back when it's growing toward something imagined, not guarding against something feared, and it stops exhausting you.
cells.core:
Something that couldn't hold has come down, and you've gone into caretaker mode on all of it — the parts worth keeping and the rubble too. You're managing, patching, staying ahead of the next thing that might give. Somewhere ahead is a version where you kept everything standing by sheer attention, and you're living there, which means you can't see the clearing you're actually in.

The way out isn't more tending. It's letting what happened finish happening, all the way through you, until you can imagine the ground as open instead of exposed. Picture what could grow here. Then choose what to keep. Care that's pointed at a vision holds without clutching; care that's pointed at a fear never gets to put anything down.
cells.sheetLine: You're trying to keep even the rubble alive. Let it land, then imagine the ground.

cells.tense: You're still standing at the spot where it fell, and the falling is over.
cells.verb: letting what survived go untended because tending anything feels like asking for another collapse
cells.place: in the clearing where something built on a wrong idea came down
cells.ask: Pick one thing that's still standing and keep hoping at it — a little, daily, with no proof it'll take. Strength put into staying hopeful pulls the care back through; the tending starts again on its own, and it grows without you forcing it.
cells.core:
Something that couldn't hold came down, and you've stopped tending what it left behind. Not because nothing survived — because caring for it feels like setting up the next fall. So the real parts are sitting there, unwatered, while you stand at a door that's already behind you.

Don't try to care harder; that's pushing on an empty tank. Go around instead. Find one living thing in the clearing and keep hoping at it, quietly, every day, without needing it to prove anything. Hope kept up after a collapse is its own kind of strength, and it's the current that brings the tending back. What you cultivate from there reaches the end on its own, and you get to be there, not back at the door.
cells.sheetLine: The falling is over and you've stopped tending what survived. Keep hoping at one thing.

cells.tense: You're already tending the clearing; you just talk about it like the dust is settling by itself.
cells.verb: keeping two real things alive, carefully, while the false thing finishes falling
cells.place: in the clearing where something built on a wrong idea came down
cells.ask: Say out loud, to one person, what you gave up to keep this standing — in plain words, once. When the sacrifice gets a witness it gets to be finished, the letting go becomes yours, and the care you're already giving stops needing to hide as coping.
cells.core:
Something that couldn't hold came down, and the real parts are still alive — because you've been keeping them alive. You've been choosing what to water, holding two needs in balance, doing it well. But if someone asked, you'd say things just sort of sorted themselves out. The tending is running. The claim on it isn't.

The simplest version of the fix is just to let it be seen. Tell one person what you let fall and what it cost you to let it. Not the whole story — the one true sentence. A sacrifice that's witnessed gets to end; one that's unnamed keeps quietly costing. Once it's yours out loud, the care you're already giving can hold what's growing without gripping it, and without pretending it's nobody's work.
cells.sheetLine: You're already tending what's real. Say what you gave up to do it.

flags.detail: "a while ago" — a cell knows no one's past
